title: Russia Bans Fuel Exports Through 2027, US Restricts Critical Mineral Scrap, and Brent Marks a Benchmark Milestone With No August Cargoes
subhead: Moscow extended its gasoline and diesel export ban through January 2027 — a sign its domestic fuel crisis is far from resolved — while Washington moved to keep recycled critical minerals in the country, and the North Sea Brent benchmark recorded its first month with zero scheduled cargoes.

sections.heading: Russia Extends Fuel Export Ban Into 2027
sections.body:
The Russian government extended its ban on gasoline and diesel exports through January 31, 2027, Reuters reported, just five days after Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the domestic fuel crisis was easing. The extension is the clearest signal yet that Ukraine's drone campaign on Russian refineries has done lasting damage to domestic supply — the ban was originally intended as a temporary measure. Russia has been grappling with gasoline and diesel shortages for nearly three months, as repeated Ukrainian strikes forced major refineries offline through the spring and early summer.

Some refineries had reportedly restarted after repairs, prompting Moscow's earlier optimism. But the extension through January 2027, first reported by Reuters and confirmed by Oilprice.com, tells a different story: Russia's refining capacity isn't recovering fast enough to meet both domestic and export demand. The ban removes Russian diesel and gasoline from an already tight global market, where supply disruptions from the Middle East have amplified price pressure.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia was once Europe's largest diesel supplier. The extended ban tightens global diesel markets further and signals that Ukrainian drone strikes have structurally degraded Russian refining capacity — not just temporarily disrupted it.

sections.heading: Iran Stops Tankers in Hormuz as Shipping Traffic Hits New Lows
sections.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards stopped two vessels from transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, according to Iran's Fars News Agency, while four other tankers changed course rather than attempt passage. The same day, two VLCCs carrying oil loaded from the Gulf did manage to exit the strait, but overall traffic remained thin, per Kpler ship-tracking data. Oil prices rose on the news, with Brent closing at $90.17/barrel and WTI at $85.94 — both up over 1% for the day.

USNI News reported that Hormuz traffic levels dropped yet again last week, falling to levels not seen since March, shortly after the US-Iran conflict began. A Reuters poll of 31 economists and analysts forecasts Brent will average $85.22/barrel in 2026, up from June's estimate of $84.50, as persistent disruptions push risk premiums higher. Ireland's RTE quoted SEB Research analyst Ole Hvalbye: 'The market has stopped trading the war and started trading the shipping data.'

Meanwhile, talks between Iran and Oman on managing the strait continue, per the Iranian Labour News Agency, but Iran has rejected Oman's proposal for joint management of the waterway. The US and Iran have paused mutual strikes for two days, but no diplomatic breakthrough has been reached.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is using granular traffic control rather than a full closure to maintain pressure on Hormuz — stopping some ships while letting others through creates sustained uncertainty that keeps risk premiums elevated without triggering an immediate crisis response.

sections.heading: US Signs Export Restrictions on Recycled Critical Minerals
sections.body:
President Trump on July 30 signed a Presidential Determination under the Defense Production Act authorizing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to restrict exports of recoverable critical minerals and materials, Forbes reported. The directive covers black mass, end-of-life rare-earth permanent magnets, lithium-ion batteries, swarf, and other scrap containing critical minerals. It's the latest move in the administration's push to reverse reliance on foreign mineral supply chains, especially China's.

A White House fact sheet cited US overreliance on certain CMMs from foreign countries as a risk of 'serious supply chain disruptions' and noted that CMMs are key inputs for advanced defense systems. The Government Accountability Office released a 39-page report days earlier identifying 60 vulnerable critical minerals and estimating that two to 10 years are needed for US industry to develop meaningful recycling and substitution capacity.

This comes on top of China's July 24 export controls blacklisting 14 EU entities in the rare earths and chemicals processing sector — a direct retaliation for EU sanctions on Russia. The IEA has warned that China's rare earth export curbs could put $6.5 trillion of downstream production at risk annually if fully implemented.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now competing with China in mineral resource nationalism — both Washington and Beijing are restricting exports to keep strategic materials onshore. The 2-10 year timeline for developing domestic recycling capacity means these restrictions will bite before alternatives come online.

sections.heading: Ukraine Strikes Volgograd Refinery as Russia's Fuel Crisis Deepens
sections.body:
Ukrainian forces struck Lukoil's Volgograd refinery on July 31, Ukraine's Security Service confirmed, resuming drone attacks on Russian refining capacity after a weeks-long lull. The Volgograd facility, one of Russia's largest, has a processing capacity of 300,000 bpd and produces gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. Volgograd region governor Andrei Bocharov confirmed a fire broke out at an 'industrial facility in the fuel and energy complex' following a mass drone attack.

This is not the first strike on Volgograd — the refinery was forced to suspend crude processing earlier this year after a previous Ukrainian drone attack. The timing is significant: Russia had just claimed its fuel crisis was easing as some refineries restarted operations, and then extended its gasoline and diesel export ban through January 2027.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine is systematically targeting Russia's refining capacity in a way that turns Russian fuel shortages from a temporary disruption into a structural problem. The Volgograd strike undermines Moscow's claim that the crisis is easing and tightens global diesel markets further.

sections.heading: Brent Benchmark Faces Unprecedented Empty Month
sections.body:
August 2026 marks the first month with no scheduled Brent crude cargoes, traders told Reuters, as North Sea production continues its long decline. The five North Sea crude grades underpinning the dated Brent benchmark will average approximately 467,000 bpd in September, down from 474,000 bpd in August, according to loading programs. The milestone underscores the physical shrinkage underlying the world's most important oil benchmark — even as Brent remains the reference price for over 60% of global crude.

The disappearance of August cargoes creates practical problems for price formation: with no physical barrels to trade, the benchmark must rely on mathematical adjustments and alternative reference points. This comes at a time when physical crude prices in the Middle East, Europe, and Africa jumped to two-month highs near $110/barrel in late July, per Reuters, as supply disruptions from the Iran and Ukraine wars left buyers scrambling for prompt supply.
sections.whyItMatters: An empty month for the Brent benchmark is more than a curiosity — it raises questions about the reliability of the world's primary oil pricing mechanism at a moment of extreme supply disruption. If the benchmark can't find a price from actual cargoes, its credibility erodes precisely when markets need it most.

sections.heading: Saudi-Led Red Sea Coalition Takes Shape as Attacks Expand
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia formally unveiled a 14-nation maritime defense coalition on Thursday, aimed at protecting shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Aden, Reuters reported. The Saudi Ministry of Defense met with nearly 50 countries in Riyadh to build the coalition, which is a response to escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and Red Sea shipping lanes. According to Kpler data, 29 commodity vessels transited Bab el-Mandeb on Thursday, but flows remain below pre-conflict levels.

The coalition's formation coincides with an expansion of the threat picture. Saudi Arabia and US forces conducted joint strikes on Iran-aligned militia sites in eastern Iraq on July 29, after militias launched drones targeting Saudi oil facilities some 30 times in recent days, according to multiple reports. Saudi air defenses intercepted drones launched from Iraqi territory — the first direct Saudi military response to militia attacks from Iraq since the regional escalation began.

Meanwhile, a drone strike at Egypt's Damietta Port on July 29 hit a US-owned floating storage and regasification vessel and spread fire to a Greek-owned LNG tanker, per BBC and Supply Chain Brain. No party claimed responsibility. Egyptian authorities confirmed the drone attack, which raises the stakes for LNG shipments through the Suez Canal — one of the last available export routes for Saudi and Gulf oil.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia is building a multilateral security framework for the Red Sea, but the threat is now expanding to the Mediterranean and Iraq — faster than any coalition can respond. The Damietta strike shows that energy infrastructure targeting has reached beyond the traditional Middle Eastern chokepoints.

sections.heading: Caspian Escalation: Iran Downplays Retaliation After Ukraine Ship Strike
sections.body:
Iran appears to be stepping back from its initial threat of retaliation against Ukraine for a drone strike on an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea on July 25 that killed one sailor. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi initially said the attack 'cannot go unanswered' and accused Ukraine of acting 'at Israel's behest,' but on Saturday Iran said it sought 'restitution' from Ukraine, not escalation, according to multiple reports.

Ukraine's SBU claimed the strike targeted an oil platform, a Russian missile boat, and 'cargo ships under international sanctions' in the Caspian, which serves as a strategically vital supply route between Russia and Iran. President Zelensky announced that Ukrainian forces achieved 'very good results' in long-range strikes, and Ukraine's ambassador to Israel said the vessel had been carrying drone and missile components from Iran to Russia.

The strike marks the first direct military link between the Ukraine and Iran wars, as the New York Times noted. Russia's Kremlin weighed in, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov calling it an attack on Iran itself. Ukraine's foreign minister dismissed Iran's threats, pointing to Tehran's role in arming Russia since 2022.
sections.whyItMatters: The Caspian strike has merged two separate conflicts into a single escalatory framework. Iran's apparent de-escalation from 'retaliation' to 'restitution' suggests Tehran doesn't want to open a new front with Ukraine while already fighting the US — but the precedent of a Ukrainian attack in the Caspian, a body of water bordered by Russia, Iran, and Central Asian states, creates new risk for energy infrastructure across the region.

bottomLine: Russia's decision to extend its fuel export ban through January 2027 is the most consequential energy move of the day — it signals that Moscow's refining capacity hasn't recovered from Ukrainian strikes despite official claims, and it removes Russian diesel from an already-tight global market for at least six more months. Meanwhile, Iran's granular control over Hormuz traffic (stopping some ships, letting others pass) is keeping oil risk premiums elevated without triggering a full crisis, and the Brent benchmark has hit an unprecedented empty month just when reliable price signals matter most. The Ukraine-Iran Caspian escalation and the expansion of drone attacks to Egypt's Mediterranean coast show that the map of energy infrastructure threats keeps widening faster than the security architecture to protect it.
